cells.tense: The pen is in your hand right now and the line being drawn is yours.
cells.ask: Before the week is out, tell one person the thing you're actually pointed at, plainly, without arguing for it.
cells.core:
You pick a direction and stand on it. Not force, not being the one who talks most — a hand that stays on one thing. When the room gets loud you can still find the line you drew and hold it, and people around you feel steadier because the steering is real.

That steadiness has a limit. Choosing is one door closing on the others, and steady can curdle into refusing anything that would move the line. Keep the direction; leave room for a second look. Tell one person the thing you're pointed at, once this week, and let them take it or not. Staying with what you already chose is the part that makes it last.

cells.tense: You are three moves into a future that hasn't happened and your hands are already around the outcome.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're currently pushing and let a full day pass without touching it — no nudge, no check, no fixing.
cells.core:
Your hands are around an outcome before it arrives. Plans stiffen into rails. People get arranged into places they haven't agreed to stand. The tightening is real effort and it isn't force exactly — more like bracing — and it's aimed at a future that isn't written yet.

What's off isn't direction. It's how much you're spending to hold a shape that has to find its own. Set down one thing you're managing ahead of time and let it be undone for a day. Catching what happens when nothing gets caught is the part that comes back. Clear direction isn't a made outcome. When the answer is still open and you can hold still, that's close to what the pushing wants.

cells.tense: The door closed and you kept standing in front of it long after it was gone.
cells.ask: Say what you'd want if no one had told you how it would go — one sentence, out loud, nothing riding on it.
cells.core:
When you're on, this is a clean line from here to there. You pick the thing and the day bends around it, and people can feel that the steering is real. The direction doesn't need volume. It just holds.

That's the face of it. What's showing instead: picking stopped. Not lazy. Now nothing asks for you, and you arrive in the middle of your own days a half step behind, direction going into holding still.

That can loosen with one small want — one sentence, out loud, nothing riding on it, and noticing it's still a sentence, still allowed. Standing still is one kind of safety and also the reason nothing moves. Direction comes back the moment you want one more thing. Say it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped wanting, and the standing still is where it holds you.

cells.tense: You're already steering and the direction is real — but you'd call it just how things go.
cells.ask: Look at one thing you call habit or the usual way and say, quietly, 'I picked this.'
cells.core:
Look at what's already chosen. The routine, the turns you claim you fell into — those were made. What you do at that desk and how you say things to people is shaped by decisions made once and left unsigned. The steering is running fine while the story says it happened on its own.

You do say 'this' and mean it. You just don't count it. Calling one repeated thing a choice is enough to start. Try it on the smallest: the route, the standing order, the way Sunday gets spent.

Once the direction is owned, it can change on purpose. Until then it runs from behind. Saying 'I picked this' about one small thing is enough. The direction comes out of you either way. The say-so is the only part missing.

attempts.check: The record says Unacknowledged direction is 'misattributed authorship,' which is not the same as a claimed motive of avoiding responsibility, and it says nothing about whether other people have noticed the pattern — so the draft drops the sense that others are already affected and keeps only drifting-as-unseen-choice. The reader could reasonably say 'I'm not drifting, I decided most of this,' which is why the Too Much cell must make the forced choice visible as strain, the Too Little cell must render past defeat as a line drawn in the sand rather than the person's memory of it, and neither cell may explain what made a person stop. The ask survives being wrong in all four: naming a want, letting one outcome stay open, answering that small voice once, calling one thing chosen — each is useful even if the reading missed. The sentence that serves me rather than them is any version of 'and you should,' which is why no cell carries it.
